clue.text: Audibly regretted being unmannerly

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; 'being unmannerly' stands for it as in 'he was rude/being unmannerly'

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the word for regretted is taken by its spoken sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: rued means regretted, and it is said the same way

explanation.surface: Someone sounds sorry for having behaved badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad-mannered behaviour is impolite or impolitic, which is the plain sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Tied up again? Come back quickly

blocks.note: first meaning: bound a second time, RE- plus BOUND
second meaning: to spring back, as a ball off a wall

explanation.surface: A hostage is retied, then told to hurry back.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first meaning as a split word, re-bound.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball bouncing off a surface springs back at speed, and re-tied things are bound once more.

clue.text: Shrink from redhead in flat

indicators.note: in means the first item is placed inside the word for flat

blocks.note: the head, or first letter, of red
flat as a drink gone dead, or a dead calm

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from a red-haired person in an apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Redhead' is not a person but the head of the word red. 'Flat' is not a home.
explanation.definitionFit: To fear something greatly is to recoil or shy away from facing it.

clue.text: Divine female, but certainly no high-flier

blocks.note: first meaning: a Titaness of Greek myth, mother of Zeus
second meaning: a large flightless South American bird

explanation.surface: A goddess is praised, then dismissed as an underachiever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-flier' suggests an ambitious person; here it is literal, since this bird cannot fly at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the Titan mother of the Olympian gods and to a flightless ratite bird resembling an ostrich.

clue.text: It keeps the food hot in dance buffet

blocks.note: the hay, or hey, is an old country dance
to buffet is to strike, to box

explanation.surface: Something keeps the food warm at a dance supper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' reads as the meal; it is the verb meaning to hit.
explanation.definitionFit: An insulated box packed with hay, in which a pot that has been brought to the boil goes on cooking slowly.

clue.text: Lithe act, perhaps, for such a person

definitions.text: Lithe act, perhaps, for such a person

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the given letters might be ordered some other way

blocks.note: the fodder, all eight letters

explanation.surface: A supple performance is typical of a sporting type.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: a lithe act is what such a sporty person would put on.
explanation.definitionFit: A fit, supple, sporting person is described with this adjective, and a lithe performance suits them.

clue.text: Trains lots of weaker batsmen

blocks.note: first meaning: the trailing parts of gowns or coats
second meaning: in cricket the low-order, poorer batsmen of a side are its tail, so several sides give several of these

explanation.surface: A coach drills a group of poor batsmen at cricket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trains' reads as a verb about coaching, but it is a plural noun. In cricket the tail is the weak end of the batting order.
explanation.definitionFit: Tails are the long trailing backs of formal dresses or coats, and cricket's lower batting order is called the tail.

clue.text: Turnkey's opportunity for a ghost story

blocks.note: first meaning: a turnkey is a jailer, in slang a screw, and his opportunity is his turn
second meaning: the title of Henry James's novella about a haunted governess

explanation.surface: A jailer gets a chance to tell a spooky tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw is British prison slang for a warder.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's famous novella about a governess and two haunted children carries this title, and a warder's go is his turn.

clue.text: Mica forms part of schooner, for example

blocks.note: is in, belongs to

explanation.surface: A mineral is found in the structure of a sailing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Schooner' looks like a ship but is a drinking vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin transparent sheets of mica were long called by this name, as in the windows of old stoves.

clue.text: Bribe without hesitation to make more acceptable

indicators.note: without means the following item is dropped from the bribe word

blocks.note: a bribe is a sweetener

explanation.surface: Pay a bribe promptly to make a deal go down better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' looks like 'promptly'; it means remove the ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Adding sugar improves taste, and by extension improving a deal or offer so others will agree is described the same way.

clue.text: Glass's guide for leading motorists?

blocks.note: surface reading: Glass's Guide, the British trade manual of used car prices
setter's reading: a looking glass that guides the drivers out in front about what is behind them

explanation.surface: A car price handbook aimed at top drivers.
explanation.walkthrough: Glass's Guide is a British used-car valuation book; here 'glass' is a mirror and leading motorists are those ahead in the traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: The interior mirror lets a driver see the traffic behind, the vital guide for whoever is in front.

clue.text: By holding right jug, one can get drink here

indicators.note: holding means the first word grips the next ones inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the usual abbreviation for right
a ewer is a large jug

explanation.surface: A tip on how to get a drink by grabbing the right jug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By holding' reads as 'by grabbing'; in fact the first word is the outer shell, holding the rest. A jug of this old-fashioned kind is a large washstand pitcher.
explanation.definitionFit: Beer is made at such a plant, and many breweries have a tap or bar where visitors may buy a pint.

clue.text: Horse bearing leading lady

a compass bearing such as east, E

explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is drug slang, and 'bearing' is a compass point rather than carrying.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal female character in a play or film, the star role for an actress, is its heroine.

clue.text: Rare Continental articles accepted

blocks.note: UN is French for 'a', DER is German for 'the'
done as in 'the done thing', socially accepted

explanation.surface: Uncommon European grammar is allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare' here describes steak, not scarcity. Continental means mainland European, so the articles are foreign ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat cooked lightly so that it stays red inside is called rare, or not cooked through.

clue.text: Tough replacing leader? It's nothing!

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a nought; 'It's nothing' is a clue-style gloss for it

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter, and replacing it means it is put back elsewhere, at the end

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tough problem dismissed with a shrug.
explanation.walkthrough: The T at the front of TOUGH is moved to the back. Ought is an old variant spelling of aught or nought.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English and in figures, ought is a variant of nought, the digit zero.

clue.text: Select for special duty, in particular

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb, to assign soldiers to a task

clue.text: Forcibly take old money with one tax

clue.text: Slipped up carrying titled woman's pickles

explanation.walkthrough: 'Titled woman' suggests a lady with a rank; she is a heroine whose name is a book title.

clue.text: Towel may be included at no extra cost

clue.text: Treat it somehow, using chemical to measure strength

clue.text: Old chap said to appear in the warm spring

clue.text: V-sign given to an NCO
